book: 031 - Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth

chapters.file: ch04 - Popular Culture and Philosophy Series Editor George A. Reisch.md

chapters.relation: The editors' introduction opens with Socrates on trial for corrupting the youth of Athens and quips that on stage before the youth of Athens, Georgia, Cash could claim he was only asking "What is truth?" It frames Cash as Kris Kristofferson's "walking contradiction" whose paradoxes generate the book's questions: how evil fits a world rated by a benevolent God, where the enduring "I" hides while Cash insisted he was always changing, and what makes a law unjust. It also presents the Man in Black as social critic lobbying officials at San Quentin and Folsom for prison reform and raising money for reservation schools, before welcoming readers with the 1969 Arthur, Illinois concert where hippies and Amish rubbed shoulders.

Butler rehearses how the Johnny Cash persona was socially manufactured: Sam Phillips coined the name "Johnny Cash" for its rebellious marketing value, "Folsom Prison Blues" narrates a prison term Cash never served (and borrowed from Jimmie Rodgers and Gordon Jenkins), and the Man in Black image began as an accident of black shirts at a Memphis church performance. Against Jung's persona-as-mask and Dr. Phil's "authentic core self," and armed with George Herbert Mead's social theory of the self, he argues authenticity is not fidelity to a hidden inner essence but active engagement with the social processes shaping one's identity, the way paper money gains "cash value" through use. Cash invested the imposed persona with value by sincerely living it (for example, writing "Man in Black" to give the black clothes his own meaning), so the construct became genuinely his identity.

Lindahl-Urben and Taliaferro stage the diachronic-versus-episodic debate about the self (Galen Strawson's episodic view included) against Leigh Edwards's "no single Johnny Cash": the hotel-room-wrecking addict and the Billy Graham touring Christian do not fit one biography. They argue the private J.R. was a third option: on stage he becomes wholly absorbed in story characters (the Folsom narrator, the man who shot a man in Reno) while a self not defined by time slips in and out of the persona, evidenced by his account of gradually shedding "Johnny Cash" after shows. Johnny Cash the public quilt is compared to the Ship of Theseus, every original piece of J.R. replaced yet still owned by him, and the modest conclusion is that J.R., like anyone making a free choice, stood above the timeline of instants and could inhabit both the episodes and the grand narrative.

chapters.file: ch10 - I Still Miss Someone The Self and Its Travels Along the Way.md
chapters.relation: Geisz explains the Confucian social dao of ritual (li), humaneness (ren), filial piety and the junzi, the Daodejing's metaphysical Dao with its unity of opposites, and Zhuangzi's tales of free wandering, then maps all three onto Cash's songs. Zhuangzi's "Free and Easy Wandering" answers Cash's road songs ("I've Been Everywhere," "The Wanderer"), Cook Ding's effortless carving answers John Henry's hammering in "The Legend of John Henry's Hammer," and the scrambled countdown of "Twenty-Five Minutes to Go" echoes Zhuangzi's logic-bending humor. The payoff is Cash's own country Yin-Yang of interdependent opposites, freedom chained to imprisonment ("Folsom Prison Blues"), sin twinned with redemption ("I Hung My Head"), fidelity with betrayal ("Jackson," "Cocaine Blues"), and a self that, unlike Zhuangzi's self-forgetting sage, must travel a temporal path carrying its guilt, yet stays on what Geisz calls a very wide superhighway of a Dao.

chapters.file: ch12 - If I Were a Carpenter.md
chapters.relation: Butler asks what makes an activity work, testing the market definition against Socrates' refusal of fees, Aristotle's Politics, Arendt's labor/work/action distinction, Eva Kittay's care work, and the split between extrinsic and intrinsic value. He reads Cash's catalog through it: "One Piece at a Time" (the Detroit line worker stealing a Cadillac he builds but cannot afford), "Get Rhythm" (the shoeshine boy singing through menial labor), "I Never Picked Cotton" (escaping work into an empty identity), "Let Him Roll" and "Southern Accents," and the San Quentin monologue after "Wreck of the Ol' 97" where Cash refuses to be told what to play before inmates. The chapter closes by lining up Kant's categorical imperative, Jesus' Golden Rule, and Rawls's veil of ignorance: nobody would choose a society of company-store wage slavery without knowing they were not the worker, and Cash, knowing he stood on the stage rather than in the cellblock, used his freedom to side with prisoners and carpenters anyway.

Lavaque-Manty and Mickey define populism by distinguishing its content from its discourse (via Michael Kazin), tracing the 1892 Populist Party platform and southern race-baiting demagogues like Vardaman and Huey Long, then locate Cash in that Dixie soil, his family rescued by the patronizing New Deal Dyess Colony that fed his populist distrust of elites. Cash's populism is anti-racist and pro-prisoner ("The Ballad of Ira Hayes," his empathy for convicts against tough-on-crime politics), his patriotism borders on kitsch ("Ragged Old Flag"), and "What Is Truth?" argues the young may be right, breaking with populist certainty about the obvious. The closing worry is the deep tension they pose with Locke's "the people be the judge" against democracy as "government by discussion": a Cash concert, like a mass rally, may stir people following rather than thinking, so populism's ring of truth is not yet truth.

Johnson reads Cash as practicing "philosophy as a way of life" rather than theorizing: his love-gone-bad songs ("Cocaine Blues," "I shot a man in Reno," the addictions he chose) honor the descent into darkness, aligned with Socrates going down to Piraeus in the Republic, Nietzsche's Zarathustra descending into the depths, and biblical descents from Jacob at the Jabbok to Jonah to Christ, while his love-gone-good songs ("Daddy Sang Bass," "Man in Black") show the turn outward through which love interrupts darkness without erasing it. He frames this with Gabriel Marcel's "creative fidelity" (being at the disposal of others), Paul Tillich's courage to be, in which love is stronger than the nonbeing of death, and Sartre's Existentialism Is a Humanism, where wanting my freedom obligates me to want everyone's. The Man in Black thus carries "a little darkness" on his back while insisting "all God's children ain't free," a lived, political-ethical philosophy rather than a doctrine.

chapters.file: ch15 - John Henry, the Steam-Engine, and Folsom Prisoners.md
chapters.relation: Mulnix pairs Cash with John Stuart Mill on the priority of quality of life over mere life: Mill's 1868 Parliament speech defends capital punishment as more humane than the "living tomb" of life imprisonment, and Cash agrees in the Folsom liner notes (the prisoner envying the cockroach that can leave) and in "The Mercy Seat," where the electric chair becomes both mercy and the throne of God. Mill's higher and lower pleasures, competent judges, and On Liberty's individuality illuminate Cash's gallery of fools, the "Folsom Prison Blues" narrator who shot a man just to watch him die, the mother-defying Billy Joe of "Don't Take Your Guns to Town," characters whose unreflective rebellion squanders rational freedom. John Henry, by contrast, exercised his higher faculties against the steam-engine and so died happy, proving the chapter's Millian thesis that freedom matters as a means to self-directed, deliberated happiness.

chapters.file: ch17 - Conclusion June Love Beyond the Jordan.md
chapters.relation: Sennett builds "June Love" out of June Carter Cash's documented love, from the "Hurt" video's staircase glance to Rosanne Cash's eulogy that June saw your potential and "lifted them up" for you to see, and the love that steadied John through addictions and infidelity for thirty-five years. He stages the philosophy-of-love dilemma between appraisal theories (Velleman, grounding love in Kantian dignity that demands respect but cannot justify loving John rather than anyone) and bestowal theories (Irving Singer, on which love projects value and so cannot be justified at all), with Frankfurt's volitional account as a side note, and proposes June Love, loving the beloved's potentiality, as the hybrid that is both objective and active and can justify loving this person. He also distinguishes June Love from codependence: enabling entrenches the addict's destruction, whereas June's confronting-and-encouraging love, echoed in "Ring of Fire" and "Far Side Banks of Jordan," called Cash to transformation while leaving him himself.

chapters.file: ch18 - And Beware of the Beast in Me.md
chapters.relation: Barnes takes Cash's infidelity despite the pledged fidelity of "I Walk the Line" and refuses the easy diagnoses of hypocrisy or lying: "Guess Things Happen that Way" voices a good will overcome by weakness, a frail human nature anyone shares. He supports this with the situationist experiments, the dime in the pay-phone slot, the Princeton seminarians in a hurry, Milgram's obedient schoolteachers, and the Stanford prison simulation that turned a pacifist student into an abusive guard, showing situation outweighs character. From Cash's songs he draws two moral lessons: charity toward wrongdoers, since the man in "I Never Picked Cotton" or the drunkard of "Kneeling Drunkard's Plea" might be us under the same circumstances, and prudence about compromising situations, as when Billy Joe's fatal pride in "Don't Take Your Guns to Town" proves his mother right.

chapters.file: ch19 - The Doors Are Never Locked.md
chapters.relation: Held reads Cash's Walk the Line retort "Well, they're not Christians then" as a thesis about redemption: since, with Augustine, we rejoice most at the sinner saved, and since the Sermon on the Mount forbids judging what we cannot know (anyone's deep character), humility demands withholding condemnation and hoping even the worst can change. He contrasts Christian redemption, a revaluation of the person that needs outside grace (Cash needed June and the Carters; nobody is self-made), with Nietzsche's attack on redemption as slave-morality self-hatred, granting that Nietzsche's eternal recurrence also revalues the past but objecting that self-revaluation collapses into rationalization, as Cash's Saul in Man in White shows. Forgiveness proper requires repentance and a solvent character, like paying off a debt; the shame of the "Long Black Veil" woman shows why; and because we see "through a glass darkly," nobody, not the Reno murderer, not Joe Bean, is beyond hope, which is why the doors are never locked and why execution or life without parole claims a judgment of moral worth that is not ours to make.

holes.name: George Herbert Mead
holes.what: American pragmatist philosopher and social psychologist who held that the self arises socially, by taking the attitudes of others toward oneself.
holes.why: Chapter 8 quotes Mead's social theory of the self as its key philosophical support for the claim that Cash's socially manufactured persona became his authentic identity.

holes.name: Narrative Identity (diachronic vs episodic selves)
holes.what: The debate over whether a person's self is constituted by a life-spanning narrative (diachronic self) or only by momentary experiences (episodic self).
holes.why: Chapter 9 organizes its entire reading of J.R. Cash around the diachronic/episodic distinction and proposes a third, not-fully-temporal self behind both.

holes.name: Galen Strawson
holes.what: Contemporary philosopher who argues that many people (Episodics) do not experience themselves as temporally extended, and that chasing a grand life-narrative can be a danger.
holes.why: Chapter 9 explicitly uses Strawson's episodic view as one pole of the personal-identity debate it applies to Cash's contradictory selves.

holes.name: Care Work (Love's Labor)
holes.what: Labor of caring for others, such as parenting, teaching, and nursing, that produces relationships and persons yet is typically unpaid or underpaid.
holes.why: Chapter 12 uses Eva Kittay's care work to bridge the intrinsic and extrinsic value of work and to frame the meaning-giving labor in Cash's songs.

holes.name: Populism
holes.what: A political stance and rhetoric claiming to speak for the common people against elites, prizing straight talk and equal dignity while risking oversimplification and demagoguery.
holes.why: Chapter 13 is wholly organized around defining populism and asking whether Cash's anti-racist, pro-prisoner populism supports or corrodes democratic deliberation.

holes.name: Gabriel Marcel
holes.what: French existentialist philosopher of participation, being-with-others, and 'creative fidelity' in love and commitment.
holes.why: Chapter 14 makes Marcel's 'creative fidelity' the organizing concept of Cash's 'love gone good': being at the disposal of and participating with others.

holes.name: Appraisal vs Bestowal Theories of Love
holes.what: The debate over whether love responds to value already present in the beloved (appraisal) or confers value on the beloved (bestowal).
holes.why: Chapter 17 builds its 'June Love' hybrid precisely to bridge the appraisal/bestowal dilemma it stages between Velleman and Irving Singer.

holes.name: Situationism (situationist social psychology)
holes.what: The empirically supported thesis that human behavior is driven more by immediate situational factors than by stable character traits.
holes.why: Chapter 18 argues from the dime, seminary, Milgram, and Stanford prison experiments that human nature is frail, grounding Cash's lessons of charity and avoiding bad situations.

holes.name: Redemption (moral revaluation)
holes.what: The revaluation of a fallen person's worth through genuine transformation of character, typically requiring grace, hope, and recognition by others.
holes.why: Chapter 19's entire argument is that Cash's music and life embody redemption, humility, hope, and the impossibility of redeeming oneself without others.
